utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Philip Weiner for the Prosecution. To my left is Sureta Chana, to my far left is David Re, and to my left is case manager Sandra D'Angelo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Peter Morrissey appearing with Mr. Halilovic. With me, Mr. Mettraux, counsel and also our legal assistant, Mr. Cengic, is present, as is investigator Medina Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Halilovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If there is any problem during the proceedings please inform me as soon as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about your stay in the detention facilities. Do you have anything to complain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no complaints and no remarks in that regard, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Well, this is a status conference in accordance with Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and also at the request of the Defence. The purpose of this status conference is to hear the parties on certain issues and this Bench will see whether we could be of any assistance to both parties. We are very glad to know that the parties had the opportunity to meet with each other on certain matters that are still pending, and on some issues there are some positive results. But anyway, on our part, we also have some issues that we would like to discuss with the parties. I believe the first matter is about the order of the witnesses and the future proceedings of this case. We might have a rough idea of planning for the future proceedings. Mr. Weiner? I believe that in your letter to the Defence, you mentioned the witness lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What we foresee right now is the first witness would be Ramiz Delalic, followed by Professor Angelinovic [phoen], Bakir Alispahic, and then we had Enver Mujezinovic and I indicated that we were still making a decision whether he's still needed since we are not using the ten or so intercepts. Since we are not using all the intercepts, other than those that can be authenticated by one of the parties in each of the intercepts, there is not really any need for Mr. Mujezinovic. So right now, the order would be Delalic, Angelinovic, Alispahic. And we are trying to, as you see also in number 10, reschedule General Ridgeway at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Are there any possibility for us to hear Mr. Ridgeway as early as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you mean prior to May 11th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any time. What about his situation at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Re has been dealing with that issue but we could contact him again. But Mr. Re has been in contact with his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are a little bit worried that we should hear Mr. Delalic first, because we have to face a weekend. I want to hear Mr. Delalic maybe in a whole period of time for the whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We were hoping to bring the doctor in, Dr. Angelinovic, but he cannot come to court during that week, the earlier week of the 11th. He has meetings in Zagreb on the previous day and it wouldn't be possible to get him in. We could try and see if we can get Bakir Alispahic in to testify. Some of the problem would be is we've already making -- we are already putting together the necessary requirements to bring him here, including having him get a visa and we've notified them. I'd have to see now if we could switch with Victim/Witness too with regard to Mr. Delalic. That could be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about that military expert? Is there any possibility for us to hear him in the week of 11th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, it's a scheduling issue. He is possibly available on the 9th or he was previously available on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it possible for to us sit on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the schedule of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is just a tentative suggestion. I'm not quite sure at this moment but we are under the very tight time schedule. I believe that the Defence case -- the Prosecution case has to put to an end sometime in the early June, and which is still three or four weeks there, since those witnesses are important. And there is a possibility to finish the testimony of those witnesses before the 3rd of June; do you think so, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's only four witnesses. I don't see any reason why we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's very difficult to predict. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any suggestions and comments, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In terms of witness time, we think that would be achievable that those witnesses would be finished by the 3rd of June. However, there are some other matters that have to be raised in relation to them. Dealing first of all with the expert, Your Honours, we at the moment do not know what the position is about this expert. If the current expert report was sought to be tendered, we would object to it. There are a number of bases for doing so. Some of them have complexity so we would need to have time to draft that objection, but it's a matter that won't be a light matter that can be dealt with in the running. It goes to the question of what sort of expert evidence can be given including evidence as to the ultimate issue of a case and that's what the current report does do. So that's an issue we need notice about. And at this stage, we are not sure what the Prosecution's position is about that expert, whether or not they were proposing to tender the report, if not to tender the report, what form of evidence was sought to be led from that witness, and from -- and on what basis. We don't know the answers to that question and we need to know it now. That's part of the reason why we were very keen to have this conference because we need to know what the Prosecutor's plans are and we need to know that in some detail. And in particular, we need to know whether there is additional or different evidence to be called by that person because he's an expert and because we need therefore to be briefed by our own experts and to prepare to cross-examine somebody in a specialist field. We can't do that if we are told that at short notice, nor can the Tribunal adequately prepare. So that's something in my submission that should be dealt with today, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's deal with it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecution mentioned very clearly that the expert witness will not be filing a new expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. In that situation, Your Honour, we need some sort of a -- we don't know what he's going to say, because his previous report, it would be common ground, was based -- more than 50 per cent of it was based on materials that came from witnesses who aren't being called any more. Or material which may not be admitted into evidence by Your Honours pursuant to other evidentiary applications that there are. So it needs to be revealed what this witness is going to say and we have no idea what he's going to say outside of that report, the contents of which in many ways would be challenged by the Defence if it had been sought to be led. So we need to know that because we don't want to object on a question-by-question basis to an expert, Your Honours. That's destructive and distracting and makes it hard to follow exactly what the witness is attempting to communicate, some of which might be of use to the Tribunal. And therefore, we need a clear indication and we want it to be by way of a report. We are not in a position to demand anything. But the Defence can't be exposed to an expert saying what we expect to be something quite new at short notice. Frankly, Your Honours, if we get prompt notification, as we have been saying for about two months now, if we get prompt notification about this, we will meet any deadline the Court sets, including the 9th of May but we have to be given the information and we have to be given it now. Frankly, because Your Honour, it just puts us in an impossible position. Otherwise we can't meaningfully cross-examine an expert unless we have a proof in advance of what we are going to say and proofing notes two days before cannot be an appropriate way to proceed with an expert. Therefore, that's what we ask and we ask that the Prosecution clarify exactly what it is that the witness is going to say and give us that in sufficient particularity to allow us to deal with that matter by means of our own experts and to consider whether we have challenges to the admissibility or use of such evidence or whether we are quite satisfied with it. That needs to be something that -- in my submission, that could be scheduled today, that the Prosecutor provide by a certain data a report or other information to the Defence indicating what this witness is going to say. Because right now, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I quite agree with you on this matter, but, however, from the previous practice concerning the testimony of the expert witness, it will be very simple matter if I could put it in this way. That is, the party calling the expert witness should tender that report, and during the direct examination the party should ask some questions outlining the main points in that report, which will last for about 30 or 40 minutes. It will not last long. Then the other party has the right to cross-examine that witness in full because, as an expert, he will testify to something beyond the common knowledge -- I mean beyond the knowledge of the counsels and the judges in a specific areas. I think this is the normal practice for the testimony of an expert witness. But I don't know how the Prosecution would like to conduct with this expert witness. Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has, as I'm sure Your Honour appreciates, had some difficulty because of the -- with the expert in the time frame because of the reduction in the number of witnesses in December, and scheduling the witness in. He's an extremely senior British general. He's actually the head of British military intelligence and is an extremely busy person. We have been in contact with his office trying to fit him in on a number of occasions but the trial has gone longer than we anticipated. And we did want to have General Karavelic give his evidence at the beginning, but we accommodated both the Defence and General Karavelic and didn't call him until last week. So we weren't really in a position to schedule General Ridgeway in until after that. And the problem was Mr. Karavelic testified for three weeks in Hadzihasanovic and required extra time. That just put everything -- it just moved everything aside. The problem General Ridgeway has is there was probably only one day he could have testified in the first few weeks of May and that was the 9th of May, and we were ready to try and schedule him in but then the scheduling order was made for the Wednesday. So we didn't make an attempt to go and see him. What we have to do is go and see him and in the light of the change in the case, or the -- the evidence, as opposed to the evidence he was given originally, to ask for his opinion on that. Now his opinion won't, as far as we anticipate, be vastly different because we are asking him to comment upon the duties of a commander in a given situation and what the commander should have done and except in this scenario what the evidence is in our case the commander actually did do; has the commander complied with his duties under international humanitarian law. That is already in his existing report and it's a matter of modifying orally some parts of that report. And of course, we won't rely on some parts of that report. And of course after having spoken to the general we will provide the Defence with full notes of his anticipated evidence without him having to do another report which, quite frankly, he just can't do. He's not in a position to write another report. So it's a matter of fitting him in and our current information is he's just not available in the next few weeks after that. So we are waiting for another day, hopefully at the end of May, in which we could get him to testify. Presumably only for a day. My learned friend also mentioned at one point the ultimate issue. I think Your Honour has moved to that or touched on that. There is no rule before this international Tribunal in relation to military experts not expressing an opinion as to the ultimate issue. That is whether the accused has complied or fulfilled his duties, because that's the function of the expert, to express an opinion based upon assumed evidence which will guide the Trial Chamber. It's the practice as far as we know in our submission in all the other trials and it shouldn't be any different here. So that's the current situation. Unfortunately, there has to be some flexibility here when you're dealing with someone of that level of seniority. So we can't tell you today an exact date but we can certainly work with the Defence as to the amount of time they need but in our submission it shouldn't be too long because the issues are fairly clear. We just don't anticipate any surprises in what he'll say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We just want to be informed as early as possible. The first issue is whether he will be able to testify on the 9th of May. If not, what is the other time? I think a time has to be set up for that specific days, and at least there should be a week beforehand to inform the Bench and the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That would cut out the 9th of May. We wouldn't -- we wouldn't have the full week. That's the Monday, the 9th. I'll make some more inquiries this afternoon. I can notify Chamber's legal officer and Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Is it satisfactory to your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say, Your Honour, it's very unsatisfactory on a number of grounds. The first one is that, as my learned friend may know, there is quite a lot of authority making it clear that the ultimate issue, opinions are not to be given in this Tribunal or anywhere else. We will deal that later on in motions in we have to but that submission is more smoke, in my submission. Secondly, we are not to be told that one day's cross-examination is sufficient. We are not undertaking to go for one day. We may have to go for more. We may have to go for less. But issues of admissibility may have to be dealt with beforehand and to therefore ask that he come along on the 9th for a one-day all-encompassing piece of evidence is not feasible at all. And the Defence thinks it's unlikely that we would finish that witness in under two days and one day I can say now that we would not do so. Finally, Your Honours, we would not be in any way satisfied by some notes of amendments to that report. The Defence -- if the Prosecutor is now indicating that they would seek to tender that report in evidence, we indicate now that we oppose its being tendered and we are going to move a motion to prevent that from happening. If the Prosecutors really do intend to proceed in that way, and they have indicated in open court that they are, that's the battle we will fight. It takes some preparation we will do so, but -- because the report, we say, has a number of flaws. They don't need to concern the Court right now. Now, Your Honours could I just make this point? Whatever the scheduling difficulties may be that the Prosecutor has encountered, and obviously the Prosecutor has difficult problems from time to time which we acknowledge, and obviously fitting witnesses in at different times is an issue. But frankly, it doesn't have to be General Ridgeway. It could be somebody else. The -- it would be perfectly appropriate to find another witness because frankly, this witness made his -- gave his report on more than 50 per cent of material which has nothing to do with this case. Undertaking the task of taking out the parts which were formed on that basis and asking him to -- with a clean slate to form a new opinion seems to me to be a very difficult task to ask anyone to undertake. But in any event, it's not something that ought to delay the trial. It has to be borne in mind that Mr. Halilovic is in custody. This case has gone smoothly in most respects and the Prosecution case is coming to a close now. We won't object to a new expert and we won't object to a new expert report but we want a report. We want something signed, we want something complete. We want something to make it clear why an expert witness has come to the conclusions that she or he happened to come to. We need that. We won't delay things. We are not trying to be obstructive. We are very happy to press on. But it's -- we are not happy with the form that's proposed and in its current form we would make it clear that we with challenge the admissibility of that report in its current form. As to the 9th, I would consider that to be a hopeless goal at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible for us to hear Professor Angelinovic on the 11th of May, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. He's going to be in a meeting in Zagreb on the 10th. We had scheduled him for the following week. He has several meetings afternoon he has international visitors. He was available the following week. I think he can arrive on the 17th and testify on the 18th and 19, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But anyway, I believe that the Prosecution's case has to come to an end at the beginning of June, which is the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The other option, if you want to do Delalic all at once, if we could possibly start -- I would contact Dr. Angelinovic again and see if we could start on the 12th. He could arrive either late night on the 10th or early morning on the 11th. That would give us a chance to talk to him and then he would go on the stand the following day. I could see if that would be feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But on the 12th, we only have two days on that week. That is 12th and 13th. Is it possible for him to stay until next week, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The 16th is a holiday. It would be into the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't see his testimony going that long. We completed the other pathologist very quickly. In fact we 87(F)ed the direct examination of the other pathologist's testimony and that's under consideration in this case too with regard to this expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could assist with that one. The Defence would not object to the subject to resolving two small matters with my learned friend. I would not object to the 89(F) procedure with respect to this witness. Nor would we object to a videolink if the Prosecution felt that could be accommodated with that witness. He's an expert witness so there is no need for -- I was going to say courtroom dramatics. But in any event. It's a very -- it's a very confined cross-examination. I think we would finish him in two days. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. But the videolink witness will take the Tribunal a lot of time because we have to prearrange it at least three weeks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, look, it's simply a suggestion. We will assist. Frankly if that witness could be by some means arranged as the first witness, that would probably suit everyone and we won't take too long with Angelinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Weiner, try your best to make this witness come on the 12th. So we try to finish him in two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. But you have to inform us as early as possible about the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact if I get an idea which issues we are going to cover next I'll leave the courtroom at this time and get on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are we just going to do these seven on the Defence list or did you have others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe it depends on how long the Defence would like to elaborate on those issues. But to us the most important is the witness list and the scheduling issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me leave for about 15 minutes and see if I can make some arrangements for the doctor and the case is in good hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope the Defence case could be started no later than the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It will last until the 22nd of July, before the recess. If the -- if possible, I'm afraid that we have to sit a little bit during the recess period, maybe one week, to finish the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate we -- I believe we would be in a position to start by then and we may be in a position to start earlier and we hope to start earlier than that, if possible. Therefore, we meant to remain in contact with the Prosecution and with the Court as to that. But could I indicate that a great deal of the length of the Defence case really depends upon how the expert evidence pans out, how the expert evidence turns out here in the Prosecution case. The necessity for dealing with the matter at an expert level is very volatile right at the moment. We do not know what is going to be said by the expert, Lieutenant General Ridgeway, on the new material and our response to it, although we have in the past given much thought to this issue and cross-examined on expert matters from time to time, we still don't know precisely what we are facing in that regard, and that is -- that does create some volatility for us. And therefore, Your Honours, I would prefer not to undertake right now that we could start earlier than the time when Your Honour indicates. I can say that we would start by then. I'm very confident we would be able to. I'm also relatively confident we could start a week before that and I think it would be desirable even though that means a relatively short break, bearing in mind the break that we are now having -- we, I mean counsel, not the judges in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But you have to bear in mind that there is a 98 bis proceedings, a 65 ter filings on your part, and as well as the Pre-Defence Conference. All those procedural matters we have to do it. Of course, we will do our best to shorten the period in between, but we believe that two or three weeks is not a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I say, we could give you a clearer picture once we know what the situation is with the expert. But we ourselves may need to engage another expert, depending on how things develop. But nevertheless, what Your Honour says we will comply with, we will be ready to start at that time that Your Honour has indicated. And as to starting earlier, we'll see what we can accomplish and if the Court is prepared to start us earlier then we will. As to sitting into the break, into the recess, Your Honours, I would entirely support doing so if that's possible. And as I've indicated in the past, I think it's -- it's very much the Defence hope to keep the Defence case very confined in this case. And that's our intention to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next issue is about so-called status of Mr. Delalic and the position of the OTP relative to witnesses. I'm a little bit puzzled with this description. Maybe Mr. Morrissey could shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are various aspects to the matters we wanted to raise about this witness. Some of them, on reflection, perhaps, are not appropriate to trouble the Court with now. But there is one matter that or one issue that we need clarification on. It's really a particulars issue in another way. The Prosecution case with respect to Mr. Delalic has been in the past that he was an effectively a dangerous criminal, and it's part of the notice case against Mr. Halilovic that he should have known better than to use the unit led by so dangerous a man. The indictment makes it clear what the Prosecution's position about Mr. Delalic was. It uses particular phrases, in particular refers to him as -- Mr. Delalic as a commander. It refers to Mr. Delalic ordering the burial of bodies, and in short, it puts Mr. Delalic in a position where he must, on the Prosecution's own case, be guilty of a war crime of failing to punish. He must be guilty of that on the Prosecution's own case. Therefore, we wish to be clear, we need to know whether that witness is one who is going to be warned and given the relevant self-incrimination warning, and we need to know in effect are these matters that have to be litigated or are these matters the Prosecution says the Defence can proceed on without argument, that he did in fact order the burial of bodies and that he was -- I won't use the term effective control, but he was a commander and he ordered the burial of the bodies. Those are matters that we need to know because, in effect, because it's in the indictment, the Defence has proceeded in other way with other witnesses without the needs to canvass those matters. Obviously there were witnesses from the 89th Brigade. We can't name them all who gave evidence, also witnesses from the 2nd Independent Battalion. We just need it to be quite clear what the Prosecution's position is. Do they say they are calling a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Does he need to be warned about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before the Prosecution takes the floor, could I ask you whether you received a letter dated 20th of April 2005 written by Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we do have that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I am slightly perplexed by my learned friend's submission in respect of Witness Delalic. As Your Honour himself -- yourself has noted, we have written a letter and I think all the issues were addressed. One of the issues was self-incrimination. That, Your Honour, has been very clear that it is I'm sure Your Honours will warn the accused of such a matter when it arises in court. Your Honour, Delalic isn't called a war criminal. He's guilty -- I mean the last I heard, Your Honour, a person has to be tried before they are found to be guilty. At this time when he's a witness before this Chamber, he is not considered a war criminal, to begin with. He is a Prosecution witness. We have alleged in our indictment - the particulars are quite clear - that the parts of the 9th Brigade were brought on to the scene who committed some of the crimes. Ramiz Delalic was the commander. He will come and assist the Court with his evidence as to what were the circumstances at the time. So other than that, Your Honours, I'm not sure how I can help the Defence in respect of this witness and what exactly it is that I'm supposed to inform them of, about the nature of his testimony. We have disclosed to the Defence all the transcripts of this particular witness, of his interviews with the OTP and other interviews that he's had, and that to my mind would be quite sufficient to put the Defence on notice as to what this witness is coming to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But what is his status at this moment? Is he still under the trial? He's indicted? He's a detainee? Or he's released on provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: He's released, Your Honour. He at this moment served his -- I think he had a six-month sentence and all that information has equally been provided to the Defence and he's been released since December. There may be other charges going to be leveled against him and this is also been disclosed to the Defence, on a murder case at the wedding. But at this moment, Your Honour, he is -- he is not in custody, and neither is he facing any charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you think he needs a lawyer during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe his lawyer, Mr. Karkin is going to travel with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Defence, firstly could I say what my learned friend says does clarify matters. The Prosecutor, as I understand, is standing by the indictment and that does answer my question. So I'm grateful for that indication. But secondly, as to the situation with Mr. Delalic, as we understood it, he has been charged and awaits trial and is on provisional release in respect to the wedding murder. That's our information and it had better be clarified, I think, what his position is about that. It might be of significance. That's what our understanding is, that he's been charged, that he was in prison for it on remand but subsequently has been provisionally released in respect of that and that's outstanding. If our information is wrong we are very happy to withdraw the comment but that's what we think is the situation from some extensive inquiries and we better that have clarified too Your Honour, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indictment has been issued by the Sarajevo cantonal court. Whether he's actually been arrested or under provisional release, my information is that's not the case. But I will certainly look into the matter because the indictment itself was handed over to the Defence in our disclosure. And as far as we are concerned, the Bosnian government is giving him a visa on the basis that he is not under any charges at the moment but there has been an indictment issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm looking forward to your answer. Well, the next issue is about the material relevant to the credit of Prosecution witnesses. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just excuse me one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks. Yes, sorry I was just seeing what the latest situation was, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution have undertake to provide us with supporting material with respect to indictments concerning the three named individuals Delalic, Alispahic, Mujezinovic. We await that material with bated breath. And it could be of significance in the case. We have been provided today with a statement. It may be that the Bosnian version of it was disclosed before. Before I say any more about that I think we will just investigate the extent to which that was disclosed in the electronic material. So, Your Honour, there has been some progress there. Can I indicate the Prosecution have undertaken to provide us with certain material as and when they get it. But it's recognised that it exists and it's of importance. The Defence sometimes has trouble getting that material through other sources. Anyway, it's coming from the Prosecution and we await it. And of course, any other material that arises we need to be provided with. Could it -- just to be clear about one matter that has been mentioned by me in the past, and I've used a general term, the term disclosure, and we've asked that the Prosecution disclose such materials. We think that there is a wider duty that the Prosecution has got than just to disclose. Of course the Prosecution does disclose material. You'll recall that they did so, quite correctly, if I may say so, with respect to one witness -- I just can't recall if he was under special measures. I won't say his name. But anyway, the Prosecutors did provide us with something concerning an allegation concerning him. He didn't agree with it. But they did provide that. It was capable of being exculpatory so they provided it. Exculpatory material can be quite wide. It doesn't have to be limited to a certified copy of a conviction. Sometimes people aren't convicted. One thinks of -- well, one that comes to mind is Adolf Hitler. You don't have to be convicted to be a war criminal or guilty of all sorts of things or have material that's relevant to credit. So that we make the point that it's not just a question of formal convictions but of material that's relevant to the credibility of a witness. And secondly, we mention that the Prosecutors, we think, we submit, are under a duty to -- once they are on notice to have a look to see what the situation is. Now, the Prosecutors have responded to submissions made by us in court in the past, by undertaking to provide what they can and we are grateful for that indication, but it may be that there is more and we don't want a situation to develop and we think we should put it on the record now, that later, materials emerge after the witnesses have gone. It's not to anyone's benefit if that happens. It's not to the Prosecutor's benefit. It's certainly not to the Defence's benefit. And it creates all sorts of difficulties and mistrust at a later time will we don't want. Those are the only things I have to say on that topic because, Your Honours, we have been provided with that indication by the Prosecutors and therefore they appear to be cooperating and we are happy to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour, that we have been meeting our Rule 68 obligations and we continue to meet them. However, the law of this Tribunal has limited the Rule 68 obligations. If the Court looks at Prosecutor versus Blagojevic 12 December 2002, joint decision on motions related to production of evidence, the Court states at paragraph 26, which is the paragraph that begins, "as the Appeals Chamber has previously held, if exculpatory evidence is known and the evidence is accessible, the Prosecution may be relieved of its obligation to disclose the material under Rule 68." And it continues: "Rule 68 is not intended to serve as a means through which the Prosecution is forced to replace the Defence in conducting investigations or gathering material that may assist the Defence. Rule 68 also does not translate into a right for the Defence to receive all the Prosecution's evidence that could be useful in the Defence against charges in the amended indictment." And then it continues on page 11. That was page 10, paragraph 26. Into paragraph 27 on page 11: "Rule 68 requires the Prosecution to disclose material which may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of an accused or material that may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. It is not, however, for the Prosecution to step into the shoes of the Defence and research publicly accessible material." If they are aware of certain charges, they have investigators, they have attorneys in Sarajevo, and they can just as well get this information as the Prosecution. As this Court well knows, if you look at the Statute or look at the case law, we are only responsible to provide materials in our possession or materials being held by the Prosecution. And we have complied with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for reminding me of that decision. But at the same time, I have to say that according to the Rules and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Prosecution has the consistent obligations to disclose any materials if the Rule 68 so long as they are at their possession. I hope the Prosecution could continue this request and research for those materials. At the same time, I have to say that the Defence could not make a fishing expedition for that. You must have some evidence to show us that certain documents is now in the possession of the Prosecution so that the Bench could accommodate the request from the Defence. Yes, third matter is the deposition of Mr. Karic. Up to now, this Bench is elaborating the arguments put forward by the both parties on this very issue. We haven't make up our mind on that particular issue. So I believe that it is premature to discuss it. Anyway, we will make our decisions as early as feasible and inform the both parties as early as possible so that both parties could be prepared if -- if -- the motion from the Defence is granted. Yes. The fourth issue is about Mr. Halilovic's interview. I'm not quite sure at this moment whether the submissions by Mr. Re on the other day could constitute a formal submission of this document or not. I don't know whether we need some written submissions. Maybe I could turn to Mr. Re first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no. That was an ex tempore response to an issue the Defence raised in court. Our understanding was that the Defence was going to file a motion opposing the introduction of the material and we were going to respond to that. It appears that's changed, and we have to start from scratch and the Prosecution has to stand up before the Trial Chamber and present its case law and say why the document is admissible from the bar table, supported by the practice of the Tribunal. Your Honour's concern before was I think when we were going to do it and the best we could say at the time was during a suitable break when we don't have any witnesses, seeing as we would probably need some hours to debate the issue fully. Nothing has changed in it that respect. We still want to argue it and we still want to provide Your Honours with full material on which you can make an informed decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's your position on that very issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think that the Prosecutors have indicated in brief that they are not going to call evidence and that they want to tender this document from the bar table. And therefore we submit that the right course to take is for the Prosecutors to seek to do that from the bar table today and then within a short period of time, we will file a response in writing by way of motion. The Prosecutors will then have the opportunity to respond in writing. That saves the Court time when we resume, and it allows any debate that Your Honour would be helped by between Mr. Re and myself to be focused when you already have in writing what the Defence says and what the Prosecutor says about it. Now, the Prosecutors have made it clear that's what when want to do. They want to proceed without evidence. The Defence think that is we have an argument to end the debate at this point. We can put that in writing. It's important though that be done as soon as possible, Your Honour, because if Your Honours were persuaded by the Prosecutor that they should be permitted to tender it from the bar table, and if you weren't persuaded by our argument to the contrary of that, then the Defence, as my learned friend pointed out in the past, may seek to go into evidence on the topic. Now, we think you can resolve this without the need to -- for evidence, but it may be that you decide against us in that regard and that's of course up to the Tribunal. But for that reason, we think it would be the best if the Prosecutors were to indicate formally now - and I'm not suggesting for one minute that Mr. Re should be compelled to present the argument now, in court - but if he makes the offer to tender it now, then we'll accept that that's being done. And we can file our motion very quickly, within perhaps three or four days, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that on the other day, Mr. Re has already submitted their -- this document into the attention of the Bench. I wonder if Mr. Re would like to confirm it or not and maybe I'll give you just one minute for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's all I need. No, we certainly -- our position hasn't changed. We intend to offer it into evidence. We didn't formally say "I tender," but that's just a formality. Our indication is that we intend to tender it into evidence. And we thought the Defence was going to put on a motion opposing it. I mean, I can say we formally tender it, subject to Your Honour's ruling. It doesn't make any difference in our submission but if it assists, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I believe that the ball is in the Court of the Defence and the Defence will file its submission to express your views on that. And after that, the Prosecution also have an opportunity to make a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we will make it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. There are some issues of substance raised. Your Honours, the Prosecutor having moved to tender that document we will respond. The Prosecutor will then have the opportunity to respond to us. And then depending on whether Your Honour needs to hear any oral arguments or not at that stage we will comply. We'll get that as soon as possible to the Trial Chamber. If we just give it to the Court deputy and the Prosecution in the normal way, the matter can commence. I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for moving it today and allowing things to start quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. The next issue is about particulars of Prosecution case. What this mean? Yes? Yes Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I will attempt to explain to the Chamber the number of issues we have had. We have exchanged a number of letters with the Prosecution in relation to a number of aspects or pleadings in this their case. A number of issues unfortunately remain unclear. Some of them have been clarified by their responses to our letters but some, however, remain pending. The first one - I will list them and then if Your Honour needs any further clarification, I may do so - but the first one would be for the Prosecution to clarify what sort of armed conflict the Prosecution is alleging in this case. The Defence wants to make it clear that we are not suggesting that this would have any bearing on whether or not command responsibility applies. We are aware of the Hadzihasanovic decision and some others that command responsibility applies in both contexts. However, and I may explain it later why we believe it is relevant to the Defence to know at last what the armed conflict is in this case. The second issue is one relating to the body of law which the Prosecution claims to be applying in that case, and more specifically whether the Prosecution is saying that they are relying upon treaty law or customary international law. From the letter of yesterday, there is an indication that the Prosecution is relying on a mix, on a mixture, of treaty law and customary international law. The Defence is quite surprised, to say the least, by this suggestion. But if that's indeed the Prosecution case, the Defence would like to know in relation to what aspect the Prosecution is claiming to rely on treaty law and in relation to what aspect it is claiming to be applying customary international law. The third issue of so-called particulars which the Defence wants to raise today, is one which relates to the alleged obligations of Mr. Halilovic as they are provided for in the pre-trial brief. And it relates to the previous question, namely what is the legal basis for the Prosecution to claim that Mr. Halilovic had this or that particular obligation in the circumstances, whether that's under domestic law, whether that's under treaty law, whether that's under customary international law and if treaty law, what treaty and what provisions. The fourth matter which we are seeking some clarification at there stage relates to the alleged state of mind of Mr. Halilovic. As Your Honour will be aware, this is a matter which should have been pleaded in the indictment and which has not been pleaded in the indictment. And we seek some clarification in that regard as well. Lastly, the Defence is seeking clarification as to the position of the Prosecution in relation to the order of the 30th of August 1993 and its relevance to the Prosecution case. There again we believe it is a matter of great ambiguity and which could have an impact upon the Defence days and its position. So those are the matters, Your Honour. If you need any further assistance, I may clarify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, as for the nature of the armed conflict, what's the relevance to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are a number of them. The main -- the main issues of relevance to us would be primarily what are the obligations that a commander would have under either body of law? As Your Honour will be aware, the Additional Protocol No. 1 provides for particular provision which relates to the duties and obligations of a commander and those provisions do not appear in Additional Protocol 2. So the question will be in relation to that matter. Where is the law to be found, essentially, in relation to those obligations, which again goes back to a question of the body of law which the Prosecution is claiming to apply. As Your Honour will be aware, in the pre-trial brief, the new pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, the Prosecution is claiming that Mr. Halilovic had a number of obligations and goes on to list them. This list is somewhat different from the list which was in the original pre-trial brief, and is also different obviously from what appears in the indictment. So this is the first reason, namely, the obligations that a commander would have in both contexts. They may be the same but that's for the Prosecution to establish, and if they are the same, what are they? The second issue relates to the status of the alleged victims. Depending on what body of law would apply to this case, the status of particular witnesses -- of particular victims may be questioned by the Defence as to whether or not they were protected, the extent to which they were protected or conditions under which they were protected and a number of related matters such as principles which would apply, for example, in the context of a military attack, and whether or not those principles would apply both in international armed conflict and internal armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting that the victims in a domestic armed conflict should have the less favourable treatment than the victims in the international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, unfortunately that's not what we claiming. It would appear to be the case. As far as the Protocols are concerned, we are not suggesting that it should be the way but we reserve our position as to whether or not we are going to say that it's the case indeed. As far as the victims are concerned, this is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to draw your attention to the Tadic's case, which has certain paragraph specifically concerning the protection of the victims during the international armed conflict and non-international armed conflict. Well, I wonder whether anybody from the Prosecution's team is in a position to give a reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We are at a loss to understand what my learned colleague Mr. Mettraux is getting at. He keeps asking us whether murder is part of customary law or treaty law. Our response yesterday was to quote back his own book at him, at paragraph -- page 104, where Mr. Mettraux's own book, "International Crimes in the Ad Hoc Tribunal" says quote, "Murder is one of the offence which has been recognised as a criminal violation of the laws and customs of war ever since these violations were defined. It is both a domestic crime and an international offence and the law of murder under international law is essentially similar to that found in most domestic systems," and then goes on to define the elements. Murder is the most customary of any possible crime, whether -- and that applies to prisoners of war, whether they are described as prisoners of war or people no longer taking part in hostilities or civilians. The question about command responsibility is answered by the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory appeal decision. There is no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Do you mean that the publications of the highly learned scholars in the field also could be the body of law that you rely on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I think it takes sometimes for these publications to crystallise and for people to gain the level of respected commentators. I'm sure in due time he'll be there, but it's a summary of the law. It's a summary of the law at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that I have to read that book, to see this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm grateful to the Prosecution for the free advertising for the book but there are two things that I would like to specify at this stage. The Defence has never questioned that the crime of murder is recognised under both treaty law and customary international law and unfortunately this has never been the matter we were trying to get at. And I think or I have an attempted to make it quite clear what we are trying to get at and the Prosecution can very simply answer the question. Is the Prosecution case that the armed conflict in question is an internal one or an international one? It can be answered in one word and we feel we are entitled to it, according to the jurisprudence on adequate pleading in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Our response is Hadzihasanovic makes it quite clear, which is a conflict between the same parties, the HVO and the ABiH, that it does not matter. It's an armed conflict. As Your Honour has pointed out, the Tadic jurisdiction decision likewise goes to there. Hadzihasanovic goes to command responsibility. Mr. Mettraux also -- our response is it doesn't matter in the context of conflicts before this particular Tribunal. Mr. Mettraux also asked about whether it is international law or treaty or domestic law. It doesn't matter. Hadzihasanovic makes it clear that as of 1993 it was part of customary law that command responsibility applied in internal and international armed conflicts. Mr. Mettraux of course will also know that the Yugoslav Criminal Code also provided for command responsibility because the federation -- or the SFRY had enacted the relevant provisions and it adopted into domestic law the Geneva Conventions. We have also explained to the Defence in our previous correspondence that it's under common Article 3(1)(A) of the Geneva Conventions which is common to all the conventions. Each of them. Whether you're a prisoner of war or whether you're a civilian and it's also common to Additional Protocols. So we don't understand it. I mean, if they could specify it, and if they are challenging jurisdiction, we think the time is probably well and truly past but we don't understand where they are coming from. I think I can glean something from Mr. Mettraux's book at page 9 where he criticises the Galic decision and its apparent mixture of finding that terror was a treaty- instead of a customary-based crime but that doesn't apply here. Galic has got nothing to do with this case. This case is just murder, which as I said before is the most customary of any offence going back pre-Biblical times, one would think. Under any -- under any culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, how about the other two issues? One is the state of mind of Mr. Halilovic and the other is the order on the 30th of August 1993. Do you have anything to say on those two issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The mens rea is very implicit in the indictment and that is that Mr. Halilovic brought those troops to Grabovica and used them knowing of their reputation. That's the mens rea. And then failed to carry out a proper investigation, knowing of the -- after having received notice of the criminality. The second part that is of course actus reus and mens rea. That covers that. The second one is the -- I'm not sure if it was the status or the particulars of the letter of the order of the 30th of August. It's a matter of evidence. Our case is that that's an order which gives Mr. Halilovic de facto or de jure command over the troops that committed the crimes. It's a matter of evidence. It's so clearly pleaded and particularised, I don't know -- and we've heard so much evidence on it, I don't know what more we can say. If Mr. Mettraux could be more specific as to his difficulty with the status of the letter we mind be able to respond but we are at a loss to work out where they are going on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mettraux. Please be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think very briefly, Your Honour, in relation to the state of mind, the alleged state of mind of Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Re has responded and probably so has he in relation to the order, although it seems to be irrelevant now to both de facto and de jure. But we really insist that the Prosecution, and I think it would them about ten seconds to tell us about the nature of the armed conflict and the body of law which they are claiming to apply. We think that this is a matter that we are -- the Defence are entitled to know what body of rules the Prosecution is claiming to apply in this trial and what sort of armed conflict is pleaded in this case. We are not interested in what might have been pleaded in the Hadzihasanovic case. This is not before this court and we think it would be very easy for the Prosecution to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that those questions relate to some legal issues, and which need some consideration by both parties. It is very difficult for me, the Bench, to make a ruling or make an order at this stage. Those matters may be brought up in the final brief or closing argument on those issues. However, I hope the both parties keep contact with each other, including to clarify those legal issues in the future meetings. At this stage, are there any other matters that the party would like to raise? Yes, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are no other matters to raise at the moment. The issue as to Mr. Karic, we've had an inquire made. We are not doctors but we've caused somebody to visit a Doctor Abdulah Nakac [phoen]. I don't want to hand it up in open court but I'll provide it to the court deputy and the Prosecutors, the document we have been given about the health of that person. It may assist the Tribunal. When you see the document you'll see it. It's just information. It's the best we can do at the notice we've had. As far as that goes. And Your Honours, perhaps -- there is nothing else to raise. The only issue is when it comes to the issue of the mens rea, I just want to add this so my learned friend -- it's a matter that probably won't go away because when the time comes to consider a 98 bis submission at the end of the Prosecution case, one issue is going to be have the Prosecution proved the mens rea that they allege? And at the moment, they haven't been specific. They've said it's very implicit and that's quite right. Whatever it is it's implicit, not explicit. They haven't pleaded it. I don't call on the Prosecutors to re-argue what's been mentioned today in court, but I can make it quite clear in court that at some stage they are going to have to say what it is because I'm going to have to answer it when I make the 98 bis response. And it's important for them to specify which one they -- what level of mens rea they specify as there are a number of different grades of potential mens rea within the way it's pleaded now. The Prosecutor is going to have to specify where they pitch it, where they say it is fixed, because that's what I'm going to answer. I don't want to be boxing at shadows or wasting the Tribunal's time with a submission on actual knowledge only to find the Prosecutors saying that that was never their case. So clarification will be needed. Of course we will speak to the Prosecutors again but I just make it clear that it's not being obstructionist to raise this. It's a matter of significance that could trouble the Tribunal at the halfway stage and if that's not successful from the Defence point of view, at the end of the case as well. It will come back. Other than those matters, Your Honour, you've given guidance about what you want and we'll comply with that, of course. There is just one scheduling matter that I would seek to know about and that is how we deal with the Karic matters because I understand it's a matter that troubles the Tribunal right now. But depending on how things unfold with that, scheduling of Mr. Karic might be a matter we have to deal with. Your Honours may choose simply to have the deposition and no cross-examination in which no court time out of what we submitted -- you remember that we had a discussion as to whether it should be played in court or not. The Defence does maintain its position that it should be played in court. But timing issues will arise if you permit cross-examination by the Defence or any other questions of any sort to be engaged in. And you might take into account the letter that we are going to provide. It may not be decisive, I don't think, but it's a matter that we will provide anyway. But we need to know about that too, Your Honour, if possible. So that could I just make the request that as soon as the judgement is rendered in that matter, that the -- we be speedily advised so that we can make our response accordingly. Those are the only matters that we have to raise at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As for the letters of the doctor, I hope you could also furnish a copy to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course we will, and I've indicated that we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I said before, that any videolink testimony have to be arranged at least three weeks before that specific date. We haven't got -- come to any conclusions on that. We are still considering the request by the Defence, as well as by the Prosecution, but I believe that we'll be in a position to make a decision sometime next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Grateful for the indication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the arrangement of the 98 bis submissions, I believe that the Defence should make that submissions the next day after closing of the Prosecution's case, and it depends how long it will last, which should be an oral one in the courtroom. Then we will stop and we will resume the next day to hear the reply from the Prosecution. I hope the Prosecution could have enough time for that preparation and there may be a short, very short, reply on the -- after the Prosecution's reply, which should be in one day. If the parties believe there is not enough time for them, they could make some oral submissions on that when the time comes. Yes. Well, there is no other matters that the parties would like to raise? Yes. It seems to me that we have finished all the matters, and I hope that the Prosecution could submit a formal list of the orders of the witnesses at the beginning of next week so that the other party and the Bench could be well prepared for the witness. So I wish everybody a nice weekend. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 5.17 p.m.
